summary: For 9–10 year olds solving multiplicative-comparison word problems (CCSS-M 4.OA.2; UK Y4–Y5 scaling and multiplicative reasoning). Learners draw comparison bar models (or an equivalent double number line / scale-factor arrow) with a symbol for the unknown, solve for the unknown in every position (compared quantity, referent, and scale factor), and — the heart of the standard — distinguish multiplicative ('3 times as many') from additive ('3 more than') comparison. Division appears when the unknown is the referent or the scale factor. Learners tie each drawing to an equation with a symbol for the unknown.
misconceptions: Adding/subtracting when the problem is multiplicative ('3 times as many' answered as +3).
Multiplying when the unknown is the referent or factor, instead of dividing (36 is 4 times what → wrongly 36×4).
Confusing which quantity is the referent, inverting the relationship.
Not distinguishing 'times as many' from 'more than' in the problem's language.
Writing an equation that doesn't match the comparison structure.

activities.title: Build the bar, place the unknown, decide × or ÷
steps: Read a comparison story, e.g. '36 is 4 times a number — what is the number?'

Draw a referent bar (the quantity being compared to) and an 'n-times' bar made of that many equal copies; a double number line or a ×n/÷n scale-factor arrow represents the same scaling relationship if you prefer.
Place a '?' marker on whichever bar is unknown.

Decide the operation from the position of the '?': if the whole n-times bar is unknown, multiply; if the referent or the number of copies is unknown, divide. For '36 is 4 times a number', the referent is unknown, so 36 ÷ 4 = 9.
Write the matching equation with a symbol for the unknown, e.g. 36 = 4 × n, then n = 36 ÷ 4 = 9.
Check: does your scale factor really map the referent to the compared quantity? (4 × 9 = 36.)
activities.insight: The position of the unknown in the comparison — not the presence of the word 'times' — decides whether you multiply or divide. A bar model (or number line) makes that position visible.

activities.title: Matched pair: 'more than' versus 'times as many'
steps: Solve two near-identical stories built on the same numbers: (a) 'Maya has 3 stickers. Tom has 5 MORE than Maya — how many does Tom have?' and (b) 'Maya has 3 stickers. Tom has 5 TIMES as many as Maya — how many does Tom have?'
Build or draw both: for (a), Maya's bar plus 5 more; for (b), 5 copies of Maya's bar.
State in your own words why the two differ, then make up your own matched 'more'/'times' pair and solve both.
Try a reverse problem: 'A blue ribbon is 12 cm. That is 3 times as long as the red ribbon. How long is the red ribbon?' Build blue as 3 equal parts; one part is red, so 12 ÷ 3 = 4 cm.

Then try the forward direction: 'A blue ribbon is 3 times as long as a red ribbon of 4 cm — how long is blue?' Here the whole n-times bar is unknown, so 3 × 4 = 12 cm. Notice the operation ran the opposite way from the reverse problem.
activities.insight: 'More than' means add a fixed amount; 'times as many' means repeat the quantity. The same numbers give different answers, so you must read the comparison structure, not just spot a keyword — and which quantity is unknown decides whether you multiply or divide.

activities.title: Sort, match, and solve mixed problems
steps: Given a mixed set of comparison stories, sort each into 'multiplicative' or 'additive' before solving.
Match each story to an equation written with a symbol for the unknown.
Solve for the unknown wherever it sits — compared quantity, referent, or scale factor.
Check targeted traps: for '36 is 4 times a number, the number is…', confirm the answer is smaller than 36 (9), not larger (144).
activities.insight: Deciding the comparison type and the unknown's position up front determines the operation; this is checkable and should be practised across varied contexts.

activities.title: Talk it through: which quantity do we know?
steps: With a partner or guide, work a comparison story aloud, answering: 'Is this times as many or more than? Which quantity do we already know — the single amount or the repeated total?'
Decide together whether to multiply or divide, and justify the choice before computing.
Pose fresh contexts (heights, collections, lengths) and parse each one aloud.
activities.insight: Articulating the comparison type and which quantity is known is the parsing step that controls the operation.

checkQuestion: Give the child a mixed set of comparison word problems to solve on paper, watching how they set each one up (not asking them to explain the type). Include a matched pair that differs by one word: (a) 'Maya has 3 stickers. Tom has 5 MORE than Maya. How many does Tom have?' and (b) 'Maya has 3 stickers. Tom has 5 TIMES as many as Maya. How many does Tom have?' Add a reverse problem: 'A blue ribbon is 12 cm. That is 3 times as long as the red ribbon. How long is the red ribbon?' Watch which operation they choose for each.
checkAnswer: (a) 8 (additive: 3 + 5). (b) 15 (multiplicative: 3 × 5). Reverse: 4 cm (12 ÷ 3, because blue is 3 copies of red, so red = blue divided by 3). The teacher watches for the child selecting × for 'times as many', + for 'more than', and ÷ to find the smaller quantity in the reverse case.
